hits.snippet:
# 8 AI Players to Watch in Crop Breeding
## Heritable Agriculture
Based in:** ** California
Affiliation:** ** Google spin-off
Among its services, Heritable Agriculture offers an AI breeding platform that simulates how existing varieties or crosses (breeding) will perform anywhere in the world to 10-meter resolution, speeding up breeding timelines.
In addition to modeling on the whole plant level, the firm’s AI tech is identifying genes that control various plant functions.
Heritable Agriculture CEO Brad Zamft notes they are “filling the gap with our model, taking the performance data and integrating climate and soil data and then we make digital twins of crop plants.
We can predict for breeders what crosses to do, what varieties to grow where and they use their experience and intuition to refine that.”
Heritable recently partnered with Paul J. Mastronardi (a greenhouse operator in Ontario, Canada) and Consorzio Italiano Vivaisti (a strawberry breeder in Italy).
Traditional breeding programs have not addressed the needs of greenhouse cultivation, but the use of Heritable Agriculture’s platform will focus on maximizing taste, disease resistance, yield and other traits in the greenhouse environment.
The new strawberry varieties are expected to reach market by 2028.

hits.title: Introducing Heritable Agriculture - Google X Blog
hits.snippet:
# I n t r o d u c i n g H e r i t a b l e A g r i c u l t u r e
X’s moonshot for advanced plant breeding is now an independent company
...
Our work ultimately led us to build new technology to advance the way plants are bred.
Today, I’m excited to share that our moonshot has evolved into Heritable Agriculture, an independent company with funded from FTW Ventures, Mythos Ventures, and SVG Ventures.
...
## A wealth of data ripe for the parsing
The flexible, iterative work environment at the moonshot factory, coupled with Google’s AI expertise, ultimately led our team to create a machine learning platform that can uncover critical new details about how plants grow, so we can use these breakthroughs to breed any type of crop to be more sustainable.
...
## 'Programming' plants with machine learning
Our team inside X used advanced computational biology techniques to decode the natural adaptations in plant biodiversity, developing machine learning models that can identify and understand the function of specific genomes in plants.
By understanding those genomes, the crops can then be bred with climate-friendly traits for increased yields, lower water requirements, and higher carbon storage capacity in roots and soil.
...
We also spent time getting our hands dirty out in the field.
In partnership with researchers and industry leaders, we ran studies across a variety of crops at agricultural sites in California, Wisconsin, and Nebraska, gathering information about everything from the number of kernels in an ear of corn to the bitterness of certain vegetable crops.
...
## Food, forestry, and beyond
From our tests, we see a path towards using our technology platform to identify and predict genetic determinants of plant traits like color, taste, water requirements, nitrogen requirements, and even the ability to absorb carbon from the air.
Now, at Heritable Agriculture, we’re working to help farmers and agriculture companies better understand the specific genomes of plants they will need to yield the healthiest, most abundant crops in their given environments.
We’re also excited about the potential for our platform to enable sustainable forestry by re-populating native tree species in deforested areas.
...
## Bringing Heritable to more partners around the world
A “heritable” trait is something that has been inherited by its genome.
We chose the name “Heritable Agriculture” as a nod to the power of plants: if you get the genomes of these self-assembling, carbon-negative machines just right, you’ve built an intervention that can scale like nothing else.
By optimizing these heritable traits, our vision is to use our technology to bring about a more diverse, abundant, resilient, and nutritious food system across the globe.
We’re currently collaborating with partners across the agriculture and forestry industries to bring Heritable Agriculture’s technology to life and advance our mission.
If you’re working on advanced crop improvement in the seed, food, or forestry spaces and are interested in learning more, we’d love to talk—reach out to contact@heritable.ag.

...
**BZ**: What Heritable provides is a comprehensive solution to improving crops.
This spans the ability to simulate real plants in real fields.
We make digital twins, incorporating soil and weather to 10-meter resolution anywhere in the world.
We also work on the ability to identify—for traits that are controlled by a few or a few dozen genes—the causative genes, and we’ve shown that we can do that with unprecedented accuracy.
...
This is where we learn from massive improvements in large language models.
Just like we know the underlying grammar and syntax of human language, Heritable now incorporates the grammar and syntax of the DNA language into our models to understand the exact bases that are controlling these genes.
So I think a differentiator for us vs some others in the field is that we provide that comprehensive solution: digital plants growing in digital fields, working on traits that are sometimes controlled by thousands or tens of thousands of genes, and developing a fine tuned understanding of the few important genes for certain traits, understanding the important base pairs for control of those traits.
...
In terms of digital twins, we’ve shown that we can simulate the varieties that our partners have been growing in new environments or environments that they haven’t told us about, and that we have high accuracy in creating that digital twin.
In terms of the gene discovery functionalities, we spent a lot of the time while we were at Google X running the full stack.
So we would identify a trait, we would run a field trial.
We would extract the tissues and sample the tissues, which is not trivial when you’re doing RNA.
We would train the model and based off of the omics we would identify the genes, and then we commissioned gene editing.
Those plants were gene edited, and we watched them grow, and we saw how the genes that we identified actually did have an effect on the trait that we targeted.
We’ve done that in three species so far, and the efficiency numbers make it very clear that we have unprecedented level of accuracy in that gene discovery model.
...
***AFN*: What’s your business model?**
**BZ**: We’ll work with anybody who wants to improve crops.
And that takes multiple forms.
Sometimes it’s as simple as giving a license to our software tool that allows breeders that have an existing collection of genetics and have them simulate new environments so that they can increase their market share.
They can mitigate climate risk.
They can mitigate geopolitical risk.
Sometimes we work in a traditional trait licensing model where we’ll identify the strategy to improve a trait, and then there’ll be a royalty on the improved trait.
And what’s really exciting is our partnership with [indoor grower] Red Sun Farms, where we’re going to create a new, improved strawberry variety.
Traditionally, when you use linear statistical models, you have to make some sacrifices.
You either have to focus extremely on yield, to push yield improvement faster, or other things.
If you try to do them both at the same time, you make progress, but you don’t make as rapid progress as you could on either one.
Artificial intelligence allows us to do better than that.
We can make more progress faster on multiple traits.
And in some cases, having the models more constrained by focusing on multiple traits, makes the model better.
What that means is that in our strawberry program, and in many programs, we’re focusing on many traits.
These include grower traits, like yield and disease resistance, but it also includes consumer traits like flavor, fruit architecture, and color.
***AFN*: With your approach, I guess you could use this to inform a traditional breeding process or a gene editing process?**
**BZ**: That’s right.
That’s why I call it the comprehensive solution to crop improvement.
There are certain traits that need breeding.
They’re called quantitative traits.
There’s thousands of low effect size genes that control that trait.
It’s not going to be easy to affect that through a CRISPR pipeline, so breeding is here to stay.
The incorporation of the environment is an incredibly complicated task, and the way we’ve solved that is through our digital twin simulations.
There are also markets that are just not going to tolerate gene editing, either for regulatory reasons or in the court of public opinion.
Now there are some traits that are really going to be accelerated through a gene editing or other targeted mutagenesis pipeline.
CRISPR is not the only solution to being able to make and edit exactly where you want.
So we also provide the ability to lower the cost and accelerate the timelines of those pipelines.
***AFN*: Who are you partnering with?**
**BZ**: We have disclosed partnerships with Syngenta; [German plant breeder] KWS; ArborGen, which is a tree nursery; and Red Sun Farms.
Recently, we received a $5 million grant from the Gates Foundation to use the entire might and magic of all of the computational tools I just told you about to improve corn for the Sub-Saharan smallholder farmer.
...
I’m going to make a bold, ambitious claim: I think we’re going to get a new strawberry variety on supermarket shelves in four years from start to finish for a few million dollars, and this is just the beginning.

hits.title: Overcoming breeding barriers with genome editing in ...
hits.snippet:
## Abstract
Together, these developments provide a path toward efficient and heritable genome editing in complex polyploid genomes, setting the stage for next-generation precision breeding in crops vital to food, forage, and bioenergy security.
...
## Background
This review summarizes recent advancements in genome editing across four major autopolyploid crops that are essential to both small- and large-scale agricultural systems worldwide.
Although genome editing has been applied to a broad range of agronomic and biological traits, progress varies substantially across species: potato accounts for most published studies, followed by alfalfa, and sugarcane, whereas blueberry remains largely underexplored, with only a few proof-of-concept reports.
...
### Precision breeding applications in autopolyploid crops through genome editing
Blueberry remains restricted to regeneration from leaf explants and axillary buds, and its *Agrobacterium*- mediated transformation remains inefficient and strongly genotype-dependent.
...
#### Shared genome editing applications across crop species
In blueberry, similar strategies have been implemented, although overall transformation and editing efficiencies remain comparatively low [43].
Continued improvements in editing systems, sgRNA expression, and delivery methods will be essential to increaseediting success in recalcitrant crops.
...
#### Crop-specific genome editing applications
##### Blueberry ( Vaccinium corymbosum )
Genome editing research in blueberry remains limited but has generated significant proof-of-concept outcomes, specifically in regeneration and flowering regulation.
The woody nature and long juvenile period of the species make it a challenging yet promising candidate for future improvement (Table 2, Supplementary Table 1, Fig. 1).
In flowering regulation, targeting the negative regulator *CENTRORADIALIS* (*VcCEN*) shortened the juvenile phase.
Although initial experiments did not achieve early flowering, succeeding work effectively induced it, implying that genome editing can accelerate reproductive transitions and shorten breeding cycles [102, 103].
While still in early-stage development, genome editing in blueberry reveals technical feasibility for both validation and trait modification.
Continued progress will rely on advancing transformation and regeneration systems, laying out the groundwork to accelerate precision breeding of high-value cultivars.
...
### Technical and biological barriers to efficient genome editing in autopolyploid crops
#### Genotype-dependent recalcitrance in transformation
Even among autopolyploid crops, blueberry remain particularly challenging in genome editing due to its exceptionally low transformation and regeneration efficiencies.
*Agrobacterium tumefaciens*–mediated transformation often yields only a small number of transgenic shoots, and these efficiencies improve only marginally when CRISPR/Cas9 is incorporated [110, 111].
Some blueberry cultivars are also highly sensitive to antibiotic-based selection: commonly used agents such as kanamycin and hygromycin frequently either fail to suppress non-transgenic escapes or severely inhibit regeneration even at low concentrations [100, 112, 113].
...
### Concluding remarks and future trends
These achievements demonstrate that precise genome editing is feasible in complex genomes, although routine deployment in breeding pipelines still requires substantial technical innovation.
...
Achieving heritable and phenotypically scorable edits requires strategies explicitly tailored to polyploid allele dosage.
Multiplexed sgRNA systems have consistently improved multi-allelic editing, enabling robust phenotypic outcomes through large deletions or tetra-allelic knockouts.
...
Finally, regulatory policies for gene-edited crops are evolving globally, with several countries classifying transgene-free edited lines as non-GMO [176].
...
Together, the convergence of high-resolution genomic resources, improved editing architectures, optimized delivery platforms, and advanced computational tools will enable the next generation of efficient, predictable, and publicly acceptable genome editing applications in autopolyploid crops.

7:00 AM PST · February 2, 2025
Google’s X “moonshot factory” this week announced its latest graduate.
Heritable Agriculture is a data- and machine learning-driven startup aiming to improve how crops are grown.
...
The newly independent startup is approaching these global issues by doing what Google does best: analyzing massive datasets through artificial intelligence and machine learning.
...
We did a very good job moving through the gauntlet that is Google X.”
Using machine learning, Heritable analyzes plant genomes to determine combinations that could improve crop production.
By way of example, Zamft writes, “By understanding those genomes, the crops can then be bred with climate-friendly traits for increased yields, lower water requirements, and higher carbon storage capacity in roots and soil.”
The models the company built were tested on thousands of plants, grown to those specifications within a “specialized growth chamber” at X’s Bay Area headquarters.
The researchers also conducted field work at sites in California, Nebraska, and Wisconsin.
Zamft explains that CRISPR-fueled gene editing will eventually play a role in making plants “programmable.”
For now, however, Heritable is focused on more conventional methods.
“We’re not developing gene-edited plants, and genetic modification is not on our roadmap,” says Zamft.
“Gene editing may eventually come, but we’re seeing a huge, unmet need for identifying what to breed and then doing better breeding — crossing a mother and father plant, not using the biotechnology to actually develop the [crop].”
**Image Credits:** Heritable Agriculture
The executive adds that the team is most immediately focused on commercializing the technology.
Zamft did not reveal anything in the way of specific timelines or commercial partners.
He did note, however, that Heritable has fittingly raised a seed round, featuring FTW Ventures, Mythos Ventures, and SVG Ventures.
Google is an investor as well, with an undisclosed amount of equity in the young company.

# Heritable Agriculture investigation — cut-off 20 October 2026

## Bottom line

**Heritable Agriculture Inc.** is the California-based independent company at **https://heritable.ag/**. It originated as an Alphabet **X Development LLC** research project, became independent in 2024, and publicly emerged from stealth on **30 January 2025**. It is **not** a subsidiary of Google/Alphabet as of the cut-off, although X was its incubator and transferred a core U.S. patent to it. No subsidiary, controlled affiliate, former corporate name, or separate Chinese legal entity was established in this research pass. [340][343][116]

Heritable is now a commercial **AI crop-improvement platform and services company** with three capabilities: phenotype/environment prediction (“digital twins”), multi-omic gene discovery, and genome-edit design. Its public materials by 2026 expressly offered designs “ready for CRISPR, targeted mutagenesis, or precision breeding,” but that does **not** mean every Heritable program—or particularly its strawberry program—is gene edited. [409][250]

The strongest product-level conclusion is:

* Heritable has **demonstrated and reportedly validated gene discovery through commissioned edits in three unnamed species**, but has not disclosed those species, genes, edited lines, efficiencies, or independent data.
* Its only publicly detailed berry program is **strawberry**, using **AI-guided conventional crossing and selection**, not disclosed CRISPR editing.
* No Heritable-developed seed, plant variety, fruit, tree genotype, or gene-edited plant was commercially available or regulator-authorized under Heritable’s name by **20 October 2026**.
* Its commercially accessible offering was the **web-based prediction platform/SaaS and associated services**, opened in April 2026.
* The Simplot–PSI, Pairwise–PSI, Pairwise–HRB, HRB–Plantik, Fall Creek, and Planasa activities are separate from Heritable. No Heritable relationship with any of those entities was established.

---

## 1. Identity, domain, aliases, ownership and corporate structure

| Item | Finding as of 20 Oct 2026 | Date | Short exact support / attribution | Source URL |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Official domain | **heritable.ag** | Current | Launch release: “**Website: heritable.ag**.” [116] | https://heritable.ag/ |
| Legal identity | **Heritable Agriculture Inc.** | At least 2024–26 | Company grant release: “**Heritable Agriculture Inc.**” and 930 Brittan Ave., San Carlos. [89] | https://heritable.ag/press-releases/heritable-gates-foundation.pdf |
| Public/short name | **Heritable Agriculture**; often shortened to **Heritable** or informally **Heritable Ag** | Current | Waterpoint defines “Heritable Agriculture Inc. (‘**Heritable**’).” The company press page uses “Heritable Ag.” [46] | https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/waterpoint-lane-leads-strategic-investment-in-heritable-to-accelerate-sustainable-innovation-in-agrifoodtech-302549948.html |
| Social alias | **@HeritableAg** | Joined May 2024 | Account is titled “Heritable Agriculture.” [38] | https://x.com/HeritableAg |
| Official status | Independent private company | 2024 onward | Company site: “**independent company since 2024**”; X labels it “**Graduated, Independent Company/2024**.” [110][343] | https://x.company/projects/heritable/ |
| Former parent/incubator | **X Development LLC**, Alphabet’s moonshot factory; incubator, not present parent | Project through 2024 | X: “moonshot has evolved into Heritable Agriculture, an **independent company**.” [104] | https://x.company/blog/posts/heritable-agriculture/ |
| Patent-chain relationship to X | X Development owned the core patent application; transferred it to Heritable | Effective 6 Dec 2024; recorded 7 Jan 2025 | Assignment: “**X Development LLC to Heritable Agriculture Inc.**” [121] | https://patents.google.com/patent/US12260938B2/en |
| Present parent | **None established; Alphabet/Google is not shown as a parent** | Cut-off | X and company both call Heritable independent. No contrary primary corporate record found. [104][343] | https://x.company/projects/heritable/ |
| Subsidiaries | **Not established in this research pass** | Cut-off | No company, patent, regulator, partner, or financing source identified a controlled subsidiary. | — |
| Other legal aliases/former names | **Not established in this research pass** | Cut-off | No filed name change or DBA was found. A paid Delaware long-form status/history document was not available in the reviewed public evidence. | https://icis.corp.delaware.gov/ecorp/entitysearch/namesearch.aspx |
| Jurisdiction/formation details | Exact state of incorporation, file number, incorporation date and good-standing status **not established** | Cut-off | Public materials identify “Inc.” and California locations but do not reproduce a certificate of incorporation. | — |
| HQ/contact conflict | Early releases: **Mountain View, California**; later operating address: **930 Brittan Ave., San Carlos, CA 94070** | Jan 2025 vs Jan 2026 | Launch metadata says “**Headquarters: Mountain View, CA**”; 2026 release says “**Located in San Carlos, California**.” [100][89] | https://heritable.ag/press-releases/heritable-gates-foundation.pdf |
| Likely interpretation of address conflict | Mountain View was the launch/HQ or mailing location; San Carlos became the later operating location. A formal HQ relocation filing was not established. | 2025–26 | Job notices repeatedly use San Carlos and 930 Brittan Ave. [90] | https://heritable.ag/jobs/crop-modeler.pdf |

### Important identity exclusions

| Name | Relationship to Heritable |
|---|---|
| **Ohalo Genetics / Boosted Breeding** | Separate company and technology. No corporate or program relationship with Heritable was established. |
| **Heritable Agriculture package/software named “heritable” in R** | Unrelated statistical package. |
| **“Heritable Architecture”** | Apparent typo in some secondary reporting, not an alias or legal name. |
| **Google Agriculture / Alphabet Agriculture** | Not an established legal alias. Heritable originated at X but is independent. |

---

## 2. What the technology is—and is not

| Layer | What Heritable claims/offers | Evidence level by cut-off | Exact supporting excerpt |
|---|---|---|---|
| Digital twins / phenotype prediction | Predict accession or variety performance from genotype, weather, soil, satellite, environment and management data, including simulated crosses and virtual field trials at claimed 10 m resolution | **Commercial software/service; partner use announced.** Numerical validation datasets largely undisclosed. | “**Accession-specific predictions at 10-meter resolution**” and “**Digital twin modeling for any species**.” [409] |
| Predictive breeding | Rank germplasm and crosses, reduce physical trials, and accelerate conventional selection | **Used in the Canadian strawberry trials; conventional crosses planned/underway.** | Strawberry program uses simulations to “**Predict crop performance … before strawberries are planted**.” [47] |
| Multi-omic gene discovery | Integrate DNA, RNA/transcriptomic, epigenetic, metabolomic, phenomic and environmental data to identify candidate causal genes | **Patent, maize publications/data work, and partner research programs; some company-reported validation.** | “Integrating diverse data types from **genomics, transcriptomics, epigenetics, metabolomics, phenomics, and environmental sources**.” [268] |
| Regulatory-DNA modeling | Sequence/DNA language models to predict cis-regulatory effects and expression-modulating edits | **Product capability and patent claim; Annogen assay collaboration began.** | Annogen will test non-coding variants “**directly in plant protoplasts**.” [160] |
| Genome-edit design | Design CRISPR/targeted-mutagenesis edits; off-target minimization, multi-gene optimization and predicted phenotypic outcomes | **Commercial design capability; not proof that Heritable itself transformed every plant.** | “**Designs for CRISPR or targeted mutagenesis**”; “**Off-target prediction and minimization**.” [250] |
| Physical editing | Heritable says it commissioned third parties to make edits selected by its models | **Company-reported demonstration in three undisclosed species; no complete public experimental record.** | Zamft: “**Those plants were gene edited … We’ve done that in three species so far**.” [251] |
| High-throughput editing | Launch materials combined AI, multi-omics, predictive breeding and “high throughput gene editing” | **Platform/strategy claim**, not evidence of a named commercial edited variety | Launch release uses “**high throughput gene editing**.” [127] |
| Conventional breeding | Cross a mother and father, use AI to choose parents, environments and selections | **Central to strawberries and likely several quantitative traits.** | 2025 CEO statement: “**crossing a mother and father plant, not using the biotechnology**.” [37] |
| Marker-assisted selection | KWS-discovered targets may be used in marker-assisted selection as well as editing | **Announced future route**, not a released product | KWS targets “applicable to both **gene editing and marker-assisted selection**.” [139] |
| Trait licensing / software licensing business model | Software subscriptions/licences and potential royalties on improved traits | **CEO-described commercial model; contract terms undisclosed.** | “Sometimes it’s as simple as giving a **license to our software tool**”; sometimes “a **royalty on the improved trait**.” [265] |

### Conventional breeding versus genome editing

The February 2025 quote that Heritable was “not developing gene-edited plants” accurately described its immediate commercial focus then, but it is not a permanent description of the platform. By 2026 Heritable publicly marketed edit-design services and the Gates project contemplated multiplex-edit designs. The consistent reading is:

1. **2025 immediate focus:** AI-assisted conventional breeding and variety placement.
2. **Underlying and demonstrated R&D:** model-selected targets tested through commissioned edits.
3. **2026 commercial offering:** both conventional/predictive breeding tools **and** edit-design services.
4. **Product programs:** method depends on program; one must not infer CRISPR merely from Heritable’s participation. [37][250][383]

Nor should “precision breeding” automatically be read as gene editing; Heritable uses the phrase across predictive crossing, targeted mutagenesis and CRISPR-ready design contexts.

---

## 3. Core patent and publications

| Record | Dates/status | Owner/authors | Scope and demonstrated result | Limits/gaps | URL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **US 12,260,938 B2, “Machine learning driven gene discovery and gene editing in plants”** | Priority/filed 19 Mar 2021; application published 22 Sep 2022; granted 25 Mar 2025; active | Inventors Bradley Zamft, Vikash Singh, Mathias Voges, Thong Nguyen; assigned first to X Development, then Heritable | Claims deep-learning phenotype prediction, explainable-AI feature ranking, optimal expression profiles and making an edit/perturbation. Specification lists CRISPR/Cas9, Cpf1/Cas12, base editing, CRISPRi/a, RNAi, TALENs and ZFNs. Arabidopsis example uses 728 accessions/620 flowering records and proposes combinatorial regulatory editing. [121] | No named commercial crop or variety; no regulatory authorization; published example lacks numerical edit-to-phenotype validation and field results. | https://patents.google.com/patent/US12260938B2/en |
| Patent family | US active; EP, JP and CN shown pending; KR and PCT shown ceased | Heritable shown as current assignee | Protects the ML-to-edit workflow internationally where pending/granted | Final claim scope and status outside the US should be checked in each native register; no licence was disclosed | Same URL |
| **“Population-level gene expression can repeatedly link genes to functions in maize”**, *The Plant Journal* | Published 2024 | Includes Brad Zamft and collaborators | Population gene-expression analysis in maize for linking genes and function [242] | The public evidence reviewed does not establish that every method/result belongs exclusively to Heritable or that it reports a market-ready edit | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tpj.16801 |
| Maize multi-omics trait-prediction work | Public description Feb 2026 | Schnable lab and collaborators | 750 maize lines, two environments and 129 phenotype datasets used to test population-scale RNA-seq trait prediction [222] | Heritable’s exact ownership/contribution and any licensed rights were not established | https://schnablelab.org/peoplepages/jschnable/ |
| X field-data program | Pre-spinout, approximately 2019–24 | X/Heritable team | X reports **14,000 samples** from field trials in Nebraska, Wisconsin and California. [343] | X does not disclose all seven reported species, raw data, model metrics or edit results | https://x.company/projects/heritable/ |

### IP licences

No Heritable announcement or patent record reviewed disclosed a **CRISPR nuclease licence**, university licence, Broad/MGH licence, Corteva licence, transformation licence, or exclusive germplasm licence. The confirmed IP transfer is the assignment from **X Development LLC to Heritable Agriculture Inc.** The CIV relationship supplies germplasm to the strawberry collaboration, but the agreement’s licence scope, royalties, territories and variety-right ownership are undisclosed. Therefore those licences are **not established in this research pass**. [121][47]

---

## 4. Crops, trees and traits

Heritable’s website said its models worked across 25+ species and displayed the following species/crop classes. Inclusion means model support or claimed applicability, **not** necessarily a Heritable breeding program, physical edit or product.

| Species/crop displayed by Heritable | Publicly identified program/status | Traits publicly connected to Heritable |
|---|---|---|
| Strawberry | CIV–Mastronardi/Red Sun/Vineland conventional indoor breeding trials | Flavor/taste, yield, disease resistance, shelf life/postharvest performance, greenhouse management and year-round production |
| Maize/corn | X/UNL multi-omics research; Annogen regulatory-variant work; KWS feed-trait program | Gene function; feed quality/digestibility; non-coding regulatory variants |
| Tomato | Kagome program beginning 2026 | Resistance and susceptibility to an undisclosed major pathogen |
| Loblolly pine | ArborGen collaboration | Faster genetic improvement; superior seedlings/trees |
| Vegetables, unspecified | Syngenta portfolio-placement project | Best-performing variety by region/environment |
| Rapeseed/canola | Platform-supported; no named product/program established | Not established |
| Spring wheat; winter wheat | Platform-supported; no named product/program established | Not established |
| Eucalyptus | Platform-supported; no named program established | Not established |
| Rye | Platform-supported; included generally in KWS cereals/feed context | Feed quality/digestibility broadly announced; species-specific target not disclosed |
| Kale | Platform-supported only | Not established |
